shoe-lifts-elevator-shoes.text: Users wear concealed lifts or elevator shoes to look taller without visibly high heels, a common workaround in height-focused appearance discussions. The effect is on apparent height only while the shoes are worn; it does not change actual stature, and the claimed gains are mostly manufacturer figures and user reports.

self-tanning-mousse.text: Users apply the foam with a mitt to get a tanned complexion without sun or sunbeds, and it is promoted as the UV-free route to colour. Its colouring action is well documented as a cosmetic effect; how natural or even a given result looks is a matter of user reports.

self-tanning-drops.text: Users add the concentrate to their own face cream so they can build colour gradually and control depth, which is why it is discussed mainly for the face. DHA colouring itself is established; the mix-it-yourself approach rests largely on user experience and product marketing.

tanning-mitt.text: Users put on a mitt to spread sunless tanner evenly and keep their hands from being stained, since streaks and orange palms are the usual giveaways of fake tan. It is an application tool; its benefit for how a tan looks is based on common user practice rather than studies.

tinted-facial-spf.text: Users wear it daily as a one-step product that lightly evens skin tone and covers redness or blemishes while the sunscreen slows sun-related spotting and ageing. Sunscreen's photoprotection is well studied; claims about covering dark circles or acne are cosmetic and mostly anecdotal.

broad-spectrum-sunscreen.text: It is promoted in skincare circles as the central anti-ageing product, used to limit sun-driven wrinkles, dark spots and tone changes, and to stop acne marks darkening. Photoprotection against UV damage is well studied; debates over chemical versus mineral filters and white cast are largely forum-driven.

chain: Fewer crow's feet, younger eye area
uv-protective-sunglasses.text: Users wear them to protect the delicate eye-area skin from UV and to reduce squinting, which they believe contributes to crow's feet and early lines. UV blocking by the lenses is a labelled property; the link to visible wrinkle prevention specifically is largely anecdotal.

uv-tanning-bed.text: Some users turn to sunbeds for a deeper, faster tan year-round, and forum posters often claim a tan improves how a man looks. Tanning itself is a documented effect of UV exposure; the appearance benefit is based on opinion, and the same exposure is the cause of photoageing.

glass-nail-file-buffer.text: Users shape and smooth their nails with a glass file and buffer as basic grooming, on the idea that tidy hands are noticed and add to a groomed impression. This is routine nail care; the claim that it affects how others perceive a person is based on anecdote.

cuticle-oil-pen.text: Users apply plant-oil blends around the nail base to keep cuticles looking soft rather than dry or cracked, as a finishing step in a grooming routine. The moisturising effect on skin is plausible but this specific product use is untested; benefits are mainly user-reported.

electric-foot-file.text: Users use it to remove hard skin from heels and soles for smoother-looking feet, as part of body grooming. Callus removal is the device's direct, mechanical action; its role in overall appearance is a matter of personal grooming preference rather than study.

korean-exfoliating-mitt.text: Users scrub the body with it to shed dead skin and get smoother, more even-looking skin, drawing on Korean bathhouse practice. Mechanical exfoliation removes surface skin visibly; claims about improving tone or texture are largely anecdotal, and aggressive scrubbing is also reported to irritate skin.

dry-brush.text: Users brush dry skin before showering for fine exfoliation and, in some circles, for claimed lymph drainage and a smoother, leaner look. Exfoliation is a plausible surface effect; the lymphatic and cellulite or body-fat claims are untested and generally described as marketing.

silicone-scar-tape.text: Users wear the sheets over raised or keloid scars, and sometimes other marks, hoping they flatten and fade. It has been studied for hypertrophic and keloid scars with mixed evidence; use on acne scars or general skin texture is mostly anecdotal.

chain: Less puffiness and dark circles, fresher skin
blackout-curtains.text: Users install them to block light so sleep is deeper, on the belief that better sleep improves skin, reduces eye bags and supports hormones. Light's effect on sleep has been studied; the link from blackout curtains to a visibly better face is indirect and mostly anecdotal.

sleep-mask.text: Users wear one as a portable version of blackout curtains to fall asleep faster and sleep without interruption, expecting less tired-looking eyes and better skin. Masks have been studied as sleep aids; the downstream effect on appearance is an inference drawn by users.

humidifier.text: Users run one in the bedroom, especially in winter, to counter dry air that they say dries out skin and disturbs sleep. The idea is that moister air helps skin look less flaky and puffy; humidity effects on skin have some study, but the specific appearance gains are mostly anecdotal.

white-noise-machine.text: Users play steady sound to mask noise so they stay asleep, and treat better sleep as a base for looking more rested. Some studies look at noise masking and sleep; the further link to appearance is an indirect assumption rather than something tested.

cooling-eye-mask.text: Users chill a gel mask and place it over closed eyes in the morning to reduce puffiness around the eyes for a few minutes. Cold is widely used for short-term swelling, but its effect on eye bags specifically is mostly anecdotal, and results are temporary.

nasal-dilator-strips.text: Users wear them overnight to improve nasal airflow, in the belief that better breathing means better sleep and less puffy, tired eyes. Strips are studied for congestion and snoring; claims about dark circles or face puffiness are anecdotal, and they are not shown to change facial structure.

sunrise-alarm-clock.text: Users rely on a dawn-simulating lamp to wake gently at a fixed time, expecting steadier sleep and so a more rested face. Dawn simulation has been studied for waking and mood; the effect on visible appearance is an indirect link made by users.

anti-wrinkle-pillow.text: Users buy contoured pillows or silk cases to reduce face compression and friction during sleep, aiming to prevent sleep lines on the forehead and cheeks. The compression theory is considered plausible, but evidence for these specific products is limited; back sleeping is the commonly cited alternative.

tailoring-any-clothes.text: Users have clothes altered so shoulders, sleeves and hems fit, which is said to flatter body proportions and make the wearer look taller or more athletic. It is a staple of style advice; the claim that fit matters more than brand is opinion, not something formally studied.

clothes-steamer.text: Users steam shirts and jackets to remove creases fast, since wrinkled clothes are seen as looking careless. Steam's wrinkle-removing action is documented; its effect on how others perceive someone is based on common style advice.

fabric-shaver.text: Users shave pilling off sweaters and knitwear so clothes look fresh and better kept. It is a garment-care tool; the idea that worn fabric reads as sloppy is a style-advice assumption, not a studied result.

chain: Leaner, more sculpted look in shirts
compression-undershirt.text: Users wear one under fitted shirts to smooth the torso and give a tighter silhouette, and some add that it nudges posture. The effect is a cosmetic, while-worn one similar to shapewear; claims about posture benefits are anecdotal.

chain: Collar points lie flat and crisp
Sharper frame around face and neck
collar-stays.text: Users slide stays into dress-shirt collars so the points stay crisp, on the idea that a sharp collar frames the face and neck. It is a clothing detail; its effect on appearance is a style-advice claim rather than a tested one.

shoe-trees-polish-kit.text: Users keep shoes in shape and polished because they believe people notice footwear as a sign of care. Shoe trees and polish are shown to preserve and shine leather; the claim that people judge appearance by shoes is anecdotal.

good-sunglasses.text: Users pick frame shapes to balance facial proportions and to hide features they dislike, such as a weak eye area, treating sunglasses as a cheap alternative to surgery. Sunglasses' glare protection is established; the advice on which shapes suit which faces is opinion and anecdote.

bremelanotide.text: PT-141 is an approved drug for low desire in premenopausal women and is bought gray-market by some men, who mention it alongside melanotan tanning peptides. It has no studied appearance role; skin darkening or pigment spotting is a known side effect, not an intended use.
